title: The First Argument
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 11 of 40
content:
Our first real argument began with a box of ash.

The box had been hidden beneath Snape's old desk, under a false bottom so obvious that I assumed someone had wanted it found eventually. Inside was not ash at first. It was paper.

Orders.

Names.

Potion requests written in a cramped hand I did not recognize and countersigned by people who were now either imprisoned, dead, or pretending they had never supported Voldemort at all.

Snape took one look and set the entire stack on fire.

I shouted.

He did not stop.

By the time I reached him, orange flame had already eaten three pages.

“What are you doing?”

“Correcting an oversight.”

I slapped a containment charm over the box.

The fire vanished under glass.

Snape's eyes went black with fury.

“Remove it.”

“No.”

“That is not school property.”

“It is evidence.”

“It is garbage.”

“Then let the Ministry decide that.”

His face changed.

I should have chosen different words.

“Ah,” he said softly. “At last.”

“At last what?”

“The point at which your devotion to procedure exceeds your claim to independent thought.”

“That is not fair.”

“Fair?” His voice sharpened despite the scar. “You propose handing names to an institution currently arresting half the country by association and ask me to consider fairness?”

“Those names may identify victims.”

“They may identify frightened people who complied once and survived because of it.”

“They may identify people who hurt others.”

“They may identify both.”

“Yes.”

“Then you admit you do not know what you are doing.”

“Neither do you.”

The words hit.

Snape went completely still.

I knew immediately why.

He had lived for years by knowing more than everyone else in the room. Secrets had been survival. Precision had been survival. Being the person who understood the risk before anybody else had been survival.

Telling him he did not know was not merely disagreement.

It was a blade slipped under armor.

I was angry enough not to take it back.

“You don't know what every name means,” I said. “You don't know who is lying now, who was coerced then, who needs protection, or who deserves prosecution. Neither do I. That's why we preserve records.”

“And trust the Ministry.”

“No. We document the chain of custody and make copies.”

His lip curled.

“How reassuring.”

“You sabotaged Voldemort from inside his own circle because information mattered. You cannot suddenly decide records are meaningless because they make you uncomfortable.”

His wand was in his hand.

Mine was too.

Neither pointed.

The distance between us became formal.

Cold.

Snape spoke first.

“You imagine discomfort is the issue?”

“I imagine shame is.”

That was too far.

His face emptied so fast I nearly flinched.

“I see,” he said.

“Snape—”

“No. By all means. Continue your analysis. Perhaps the Ministry should employ you as a specialist in motives you have invented.”

“I didn't invent—”

“You have known me for eleven days.”

“I know what burning evidence looks like.”

“And I know what happened to people whose names appeared on lists during the war.”

The room went silent.

That was the truth I had not made room for.

Snape lowered his wand.

“Do you?” he asked.

No sarcasm now.

Only contempt.

I lowered mine.

“No.”

He laughed once without humor.

“At least we have established a boundary to your expertise.”

He turned away.

I hated him for making me feel small.

I hated myself more because part of me knew I had earned it.

But he had still tried to burn the records.

“I'm copying them,” I said.

He stopped.

“Every page. One set stays sealed at Hogwarts under McGonagall. One goes to Kingsley with a restriction that no names are acted on without corroborating evidence.”

“You believe Ministers obey restrictions?”

“I believe paper trails make abuses harder to hide.”

“Naive.”

“Maybe.”

He looked back at me.

“And the originals?”

“Locked in evidence storage until there is a formal ruling.”

His jaw tightened.

“No public release.”

“Agreed.”

“No press access.”

“Agreed.”

“No junior clerk copying names into some searchable index.”

“I'll insist.”

“You cannot guarantee it.”

“No.”

The answer frustrated him.

It was also the only honest one.

For a moment I thought he would walk out.

Instead he sat.

His hand went to his throat.

The argument had cost him.

I hated that too.

“I shouldn't have said shame like that,” I said.

He looked up.

“I think shame is part of it. But I used it to win.”

His expression remained hard.

“Yes.”

“I'm sorry.”

He said nothing.

I continued, because apology without repair was only noise.

“I should have asked what you were protecting.”

“And if I had refused to answer?”

“Then I still would have stopped you burning the papers.”

A pause.

“Consistent,” he said.

“Annoying?”

“Profoundly.”

The temperature in the room rose by a fraction.

I sat across from him.

“Who are you protecting?”

Snape looked at the sealed box.

“Some of those requests came from people pretending compliance while passing information to the resistance. Some came from people who were threatened through family. Some came from cowards. Some from true believers. A signature alone will not tell you which.”

“Do you know?”

“Some.”

“Would you annotate the copies?”

His eyes narrowed.

“You want my judgment attached to evidence.”

“I want context attached to names.”

“That is dangerous.”

“So is absence of context.”

He considered.

Then he reached for a quill.

“One condition.”

“Which is?”

“My notes remain sealed until the Ministry hearing.”

“Done.”

He began with the first page.

I made copies while he spoke.

“Coerced. Husband detained.”

I wrote.

“Unknown allegiance. Supplied information twice, both times accurate.”

I wrote.

“Committed enthusiastically. Do not trust later claims of coercion.”

I wrote.

“Dead.”

I wrote.

“Child threatened.”

I paused.

Snape's face had gone flat again.

“How old?” I asked.

“Seven.”

My stomach turned.

I wrote.

The work lasted until dusk.

It changed the box.

What had looked like a list of collaborators became a map of pressure, choices, cowardice, courage, compromise, and fear.

It changed the argument too.

I had been right that the records mattered.

Snape had been right that records without context could become weapons.

I disliked sharing correctness with him.

He seemed equally displeased.

When the final page was copied, I removed the containment charm.

The half-burned top sheets lay black around the edges.

Snape touched one with two fingers.

“I should not have tried to destroy them.”

I looked at him.

He kept his eyes on the paper.

“That was nearly an apology.”

“It was an observation.”

“Of course.”

His mouth twitched.

Then he added, “I am not sorry I wanted to.”

“I don't need you to be.”

That made him look at me.

I sealed the originals in a fresh box.

“Wanting to burn them and choosing not to are different things.”

“An unexpectedly generous distinction.”

“Don't get used to it.”

“I had no intention.”

We carried the evidence upstairs together.

At McGonagall's office, Snape stopped before the gargoyle.

“You will explain the restrictions.”

“We will.”

He glanced at me.

The word had slipped out naturally.

We.

Neither of us corrected it.

The first argument did not make us closer in the pleasant way stories often promise.

I was still angry.

So was he.

But afterward, I trusted him a little more.

Not because he had been right.

The argument had begun because he had moved a sealed box without telling me. It had become something larger when I accused him of treating every collaboration like a temporary truce.

Now, standing outside Minerva's office, the anger had burned down far enough for me to inspect what remained.

“You expected me to leave,” I said.

Snape's gaze sharpened. “At several points I hoped you would.”

“Not what I meant.”

He knew.

The silence stretched.

“At some point,” he said, “people generally decide that difficulty is evidence of malice.”

“Sometimes it is.”

“Yes.”

“And sometimes you're just difficult.”

His eyebrow lifted.

“I can work with difficult,” I said. “I cannot work with hidden hazards.”

“That distinction is absurdly narrow.”

“It is extremely useful.”

He looked down at the evidence case in his hand.

“I will inform you before moving sealed materials.”

“Even when you think my objection is stupid?”

“Especially then, apparently.”

I nodded. “Good.”

His gaze met mine. “And you will not interpret every refusal to explain my personal history as operational deception.”

That was fair enough to annoy me.

“Fine.”

Something eased between us. Not peace. Terms.

Because he had been wrong, had known it, and stayed in the room.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
